$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2{x}^{4}+6{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{-2(1)^{4}+6(1)^{2}-4}{(1)^{2}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-2{x}^{4}+6{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{-2({x}^{4}-3{x}^{2}+2)}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{-2({x}^{2}-2)({x}^{2}-1)}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =-2({x}^{2}-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2{x}^{4}+6{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\,-2({x}^{2}-2) \\  & =-2(1-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2b3845e7-e81e-5c5b-85b8-7d7f11e07468"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 3}\frac{{y}^{2}+3y-18}{{y}^{2}-3y}.$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{{y}^{2}+3y-18}{{y}^{2}-3y} & =\frac{{3}^{2}+3(3)-18}{{3}^{2}-3(3)}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}+3y-18}{{y}^{2}-3y} & =\frac{(y+6)(y-3)}{y(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{y+6}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{{y}^{2}+3y-18}{{y}^{2}-3y} & ={lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{y+6}{y} \\  & =\frac{3+6}{3} \\  & =\frac{9}{3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be118eae-f956-5136-8758-541234de46d4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-be118eae-f956-5136-8758-541234de46d4" :answer-field/id #uuid "be118eae-f956-5136-8758-541234de46d4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-89b85bb3-22c0-5d24-a29b-0c275ecfe2a8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e10ffd2c-df31-5361-8cae-6b39de43c35c" "answer-d56cb5bc-4d9d-5419-a948-dca0397cf746" "answer-81e207e3-fbc2-5800-abe0-1ceefd387562" "answer-89b85bb3-22c0-5d24-a29b-0c275ecfe2a8" "answer-4c83a02a-d899-55c8-a94f-5215ee121e17"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e10ffd2c-df31-5361-8cae-6b39de43c35c" :answer/id #uuid "e10ffd2c-df31-5361-8cae-6b39de43c35c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d56cb5bc-4d9d-5419-a948-dca0397cf746" :answer/id #uuid "d56cb5bc-4d9d-5419-a948-dca0397cf746" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-81e207e3-fbc2-5800-abe0-1ceefd387562" :answer/id #uuid "81e207e3-fbc2-5800-abe0-1ceefd387562" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89b85bb3-22c0-5d24-a29b-0c275ecfe2a8" :answer/id #uuid "89b85bb3-22c0-5d24-a29b-0c275ecfe2a8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c83a02a-d899-55c8-a94f-5215ee121e17" :answer/id #uuid "4c83a02a-d899-55c8-a94f-5215ee121e17" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5986bf81-4caa-5e55-8c99-36ab322d7c9c" :question/id #uuid "5986bf81-4caa-5e55-8c99-36ab322d7c9c" :question/math-academy-id "q-313149" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x-14}{x+2} & =\frac{(-2)^{2}-5(-2)-14}{-2+2} \\  & =\frac{4+10-14}{0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x-14}{x+2} & =\frac{(x-7)(x+2)}{x+2} \\  & =x-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}(x-7) & =(-2)-7 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dd8d554e-6195-547e-bcb1-ff6fe5d58358"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "q-37508" :question/problem "Given that $3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+5x-2=-2+5x,$ solve for $x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+5x-2 & =-2+5x \\ 3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-2 & =-2 \\ 3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of ${x}^{2}.$ We can factor out the ${x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(3x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ and $x=\frac{1}{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-10{x}^{2}-60x & =15x \\ 5{x}^{3}-10{x}^{2}-75x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-10{x}^{2}-75x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-2x-15) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-2x-15$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-2x-15) & =0 \\ 5x(x-5)(x+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0,\frac{3}{2}) & ={\sum }_{x\le 0}{\sum }_{y\le 3/2}f(x,y) \\  & =f(-1,-1)+f(-1,0)+f(-1,1) \\  & =0.15+0.25+0.05 \\  & =0.45.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x>6,y>3.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,2,4,6\}\times \{0,1,3\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x>6$ and $y>3,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/63/6340ca35646830558631c7fe523698a201c5acf26d1360910ab207c30f92e41f.png)

Since every value in the support of $X$ is at most $6$ and $x>6,$ every possible value of $X$ satisfies $X\le x.$ Similarly, every value in the support of $Y$ is at most $3$ and $y>3,$ so every possible value of $Y$ satisfies $Y\le y.$

Therefore, the region $Δ$ contains the entire joint support, and

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)=1.

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(12,6)=0.81,\,F(12,4)=0.3,\,F(6,6)=0.17,\,F(6,4)=0.1,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{3,6,9,12,15\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10\}.
$$

Find $P(6<X\le 12,4<Y\le 6).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12,15\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/71/715408bbd41d8551b8eadce9df6259f763ec34a702d48f4d116c4164ae5fda50.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/5c/5c50878b85d26a87d6220a99f6fbe896925a6802801117239a5ba56dcba46906.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(12,6).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(12,4)$ and $(6,6).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(6,4).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6<X\le 12,4<Y\le 6) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(12,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 12,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(12,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 12,Y\le 4)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 4)}} \\  & =F(12,6)-F(12,4)-F(6,6)+F(6,4) \\  & =0.81-0.3-0.17+0.1 \\  & =0.44.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ae6858ed-d55f-5582-9a7a-b52918f5e984"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ae6858ed-d55f-5582-9a7a-b52918f5e984" :answer-field/id #uuid "ae6858ed-d55f-5582-9a7a-b52918f5e984" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-69f4e30b-18e4-5e25-a6a3-ffb549051e5b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9a174190-9537-5d36-b34c-3e8b4bfbf746" "answer-69f4e30b-18e4-5e25-a6a3-ffb549051e5b" "answer-59bd9871-2a7f-5de2-add3-53cd919ee2ba" "answer-cf275f78-c17a-5602-b369-6cab88bf4a23" "answer-29f55ae2-05c7-5d26-bce8-25fa4117146b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a174190-9537-5d36-b34c-3e8b4bfbf746" :answer/id #uuid "9a174190-9537-5d36-b34c-3e8b4bfbf746" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.33" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-69f4e30b-18e4-5e25-a6a3-ffb549051e5b" :answer/id #uuid "69f4e30b-18e4-5e25-a6a3-ffb549051e5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.44" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-59bd9871-2a7f-5de2-add3-53cd919ee2ba" :answer/id #uuid "59bd9871-2a7f-5de2-add3-53cd919ee2ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.47" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf275f78-c17a-5602-b369-6cab88bf4a23" :answer/id #uuid "cf275f78-c17a-5602-b369-6cab88bf4a23" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.57" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-29f55ae2-05c7-5d26-bce8-25fa4117146b" :answer/id #uuid "29f55ae2-05c7-5d26-bce8-25fa4117146b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.65" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-560539a1-a567-51bf-978e-83db525442bc" :question/id #uuid "560539a1-a567-51bf-978e-83db525442bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-146465" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. - The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,3,5,7,9\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10\}.

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

#uuid "dc22d572-0b94-5462-9d85-2c1d61a16284" :question/math-academy-id "q-34999" :question/problem "![](images/39/39c2c86e1fca1dbcf80435237ba31fc4aed9ed8213578b4c5f3971408da59f2d.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=3$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0$ from the left and right we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)=3,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement II is false. We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)=\text{DNE},\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)=3\,.
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement III is true.  We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-{1}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-{1}^{+}}f(x)=2
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=2.$ Meanwhile, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x)=2
$$

 
Hence ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=2.$ Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x).$

In conclusion, only statement III is true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9725b865-33c5-5170-8ad4-3ac184e816c2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9725b865-33c5-5170-8ad4-3ac184e816c2" :answer-field/id #uuid "9725b865-33c5-5170-8ad4-3ac184e816c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-89743f02-1d9f-5884-b7b0-ec422e07ca6d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3cc06de8-5221-52fa-920c-03c18a05eb1f" "answer-31a4015c-7e0e-59a8-af52-660a728632ca" "answer-476e139f-e45f-5859-b5d8-144735e49388" "answer-77c0f144-34b3-52df-ac81-d4928b60dca1" "answer-89743f02-1d9f-5884-b7b0-ec422e07ca6d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3cc06de8-5221-52fa-920c-03c18a05eb1f" :answer/id #uuid "3cc06de8-5221-52fa-920c-03c18a05eb1f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-31a4015c-7e0e-59a8-af52-660a728632ca" :answer/id #uuid "31a4015c-7e0e-59a8-af52-660a728632ca" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-476e139f-e45f-5859-b5d8-144735e49388" :answer/id #uuid "476e139f-e45f-5859-b5d8-144735e49388" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-77c0f144-34b3-52df-ac81-d4928b60dca1" :answer/id #uuid "77c0f144-34b3-52df-ac81-d4928b60dca1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89743f02-1d9f-5884-b7b0-ec422e07ca6d" :answer/id #uuid "89743f02-1d9f-5884-b7b0-ec422e07ca6d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078963 :question/problem "![](images/d9/d9e89a9b811bdc6b766b01eecf817df48968e3ea604b89bc55bc9660331194e0.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=4$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE}$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,3}f(x)=1$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-{1}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-{1}^{+}}f(x)=3\,.
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=3.$

- Statement II is true. Both limits ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)$ do not exist because the function $f(x)$ is not given in the interval $(0,2].$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

- Statement III is true. We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{3}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{3}^{+}}f(x)=1\,.
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,3}f(x)=1.$

In conclusion, only statements II and III are true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186076556 :answer-field/correct 17592186076559 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078509 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-069bdd21-6b0e-5746-9f9a-48c390ea491e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-069bdd21-6b0e-5746-9f9a-48c390ea491e" :question/id #uuid "069bdd21-6b0e-5746-9f9a-48c390ea491e" :question/math-academy-id "q-67539" :question/problem "![](images/1e/1e40e0ffa7880b3b3b63070f063de207dcfafbdbed5fdf02464e180feba715e2.png)

The function  $y=f(x)$ is defined on $x\in (-\frac{5}{2},3).$ Find ${lim}_{x\to \,3}f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we see that it is not possible to approach $x=3$ from the right. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{3}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

When we approach $x=3$ from the left, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{3}^{-}}f(x)=0\,.

$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{artanh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{5}{2\sqrt{x^2-1}} + 2x \right) \textrm d x
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{5}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}+2x)\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x+\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167020 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "activity-1ab91b77-5a38-545c-aad3-8c7b75ae2ef4" :activity/id #uuid $Q(x)=5{x}_{1}^{2}-16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $25{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=5$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],
$$

To eliminate a radical in an expression's denominator, we can use a process known as **rationalizing the denominator**.

To rationalize the denominator, we need to multiply both the numerator and denominator by the radical that we wish to remove from the denominator.

For instance, to rationalize the denominator in the expression

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}},
$$

all we need to do is multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{x}$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\cdot \,\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{x}}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{x}}{x} & \end{aligned}
$$

We see that the final expression no longer has a radical in the denominator. Thus, the denominator has been rationalized.

**Note:** Because we multiplied the numerator and denominator by the same amount, the resulting expression $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{x}$ is equivalent to the original fraction $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ They are equivalent, even though they are written differently." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078633 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079505 :step/math-academy-id 653769 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079506 :step/math-academy-id 653770 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079507 :step/math-academy-id 653774 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079508 :step/math-academy-id 653778 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064314 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1e9c32a8-c5ef-5dca-8493-0a63cb017fc2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1e9c32a8-c5ef-5dca-8493-0a63cb017fc2" :question/id #uuid "1e9c32a8-c5ef-5dca-8493-0a63cb017fc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-143512" :question/problem "| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.1$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ |

Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{101}$ be a random sample of size $n=101$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $2.5$ and $3.$

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=101,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.7+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+1.4+0.4+0.8 \\  & =2.6,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{2.6}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.8+1.6+6.4)-6.76 \\  & =4.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.6,\frac{4.04}{101}) \\  & ∼N(2.6,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3) & ≈P(\frac{2.5-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}<Z<\frac{3-2.6}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(-0.5<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(2.5<\overset{―}{X}<3)=Φ(2)-Φ(-0.5).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-64ef3aa0-5b31-5f1c-8e8c-420a16ef0aa2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "e4d56835-15e1-5dd9-b189-b250c69cae71" :question/math-academy-id "q-334717" :question/problem "For which of the following values is the modified Euler method stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation?

I. $\lambda Δx=0.3$

II. $\lambda Δx=1.1$

III. $\lambda Δx=1.7$

IV. $\lambda Δx=2.9$

*Hint: The stability function $R$ of the modified Euler method is given by*

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{2}}{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the modified Euler method is

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{2}}{2}.
$$

Let's check the stability of the modified Euler method for each of the given values in turn.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.3)| & =|1-0.3+\frac{(0.3)^{2}}{2}| \\  & =|\frac{149}{200}| \\  & =0.745<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the modified Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=1.1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(1.1)| & =|1-1.1+\frac{(1.1)^{2}}{2}| \\  & =|\frac{101}{200}| \\  & =0.505<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the modified Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=1.7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(1.7)| & =|1-1.7+\frac{(1.7)^{2}}{2}| \\  & =|\frac{149}{200}| \\  & =0.745<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the modified Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=2.9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(2.9)| & =|1-2.9+\frac{(2.9)^{2}}{2}| \\  & =|\frac{461}{200}| \\  & =2.305>1.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *outside* the stability region, the modified Euler method is unstable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only".

Note that the stability region of the modified Euler method is $0<\lambda Δx<2,$ so it is not absolutely stable." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields - $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite leg}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}}$

- $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\textrm{adjacent leg}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}}$

- $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite leg}}{\textrm{adjacent leg}}$

First, notice that we are given the length of the leg $\overline{MO}$ opposite the given angle $\angle{N}$ and wish to find the length of the hypotenuse $\overline{NO}.$

The trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite leg to the hypotenuse is *sine*. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(m∠N) & =\frac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({32}^{∘}) & =\frac{20}{NO} \\ NO\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡({32}^{∘}) & =20 \\ NO & =\frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({32}^{∘})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator to evaluate the trigonometric ratio, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}NO & =\frac{20}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({32}^{∘})} \\  & =\frac{20}{(0.529\,91…)} \\  & =37.741\,59… \\  & ≈37.7,\end{aligned}
$$

However, the question of which ratio to use depends on what side is given and what side is unknown. 

![](images/8b/8b123fed4a9a42ceb69f3a6ff68ed89f27ae42294137f0cd12a9232d329d77b0.png)

In the triangle above, we are given an angle $\theta = 42^\circ,$ and the length of the hypotenuse is given but the length of the side opposite is unknown.

So, we need to choose the trigonometric ratio that relates the opposite side to the hypotenuse. This is sine, and now we can just set up the ratio, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} \\  & =\frac{x}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we simply solve for the unknown value $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} & =\frac{x}{8} \\ x & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡{42}^{∘} \\  & =8(0.669\,13...) \\  & =5.353\,04... \\  & ≈5.4,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

Note that we used a calculator to evaluate $\sin(42^\circ).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078654 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133886 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-881df761-fca2-5afa-aea8-d6a6e63a7521"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-881df761-fca2-5afa-aea8-d6a6e63a7521" :question/id #uuid "881df761-fca2-5afa-aea8-d6a6e63a7521" :question/math-academy-id "q-126866" :question/problem "![](images/0f/0f1dd3c66e3bf7d25f286720b360d6af1d6361804ab3ff52835d94f78e5084ee.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}-3y\,dx+2x\,dy,$ where $D$ is the region shown above." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-3y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-3y\,dx+2x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(-3))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}5\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =5\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =5\cdot ({4}^{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2}{2}) \\  & =5\cdot (16-2) \\  & =5\cdot 14 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69041780-f401-5aab-a5e0-f58cc39dca02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078194 :question/problem "What is the common difference of the following arithmetic sequence?

$$
7,\: 2,\: -3,\: -8,\: \ldots
$$" :question/worked-solution "The common difference $d$ of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common difference for our sequence is

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078421 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8dd21bc7-cc1c-556a-83c5-25089927d9b3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078179 :question/problem "Which of the three sequences below are arithmetic sequences?

II. $5, \: 2, \: -1, \: -4, \: \ldots$

III. $2, \: 5, \: 8, \: 12, \: \ldots$" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether each sequence is an arithmetic sequence, we need to look at the jumps between terms in the sequence. If the jumps are the same, then they indeed represent a common difference of an arithmetic sequence.

- In sequence I, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence I is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2.$

![](images/17/17933a1cabd8d487dd1607f7ae7064d6e186e3454a52497977f866150c491f25.png)

- In sequence II, the jumps are all the same. Therefore, sequence II is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-3.$

- In sequence III, the jumps are not all the same. Therefore, sequence III is not an arithmetic sequence.

![](images/2b/2b860338be6ff8876c1368ed5f08162096873fa9992a9e88d7ff545752a5bd36.png)

In conclusion, only sequences I and II are arithmetic sequences." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078422 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b7af1a90-ae65-5ea4-82bf-4487562443e4" "question-d4919d08-0fd6-56c9-962f-b38905295542"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078180 :question/problem "What is the $8$th term of the following arithmetic sequence?

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic secant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,[-3\,\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x)] \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,[\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x)] \\  & =-3\cdot [-\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}]\cdot (2x)^{′} \\  & =\frac{3}{2x\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{3}{x\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8b26d762-7065-5240-845a-7fa72921023d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8b26d762-7065-5240-845a-7fa72921023d" :answer-field/id #uuid "8b26d762-7065-5240-845a-7fa72921023d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8fa9e367-921c-5703-b5c8-f4ef0ec283c5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8fa9e367-921c-5703-b5c8-f4ef0ec283c5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8fa9e367-921c-5703-b5c8-f4ef0ec283c5" :answer/id #uuid "8fa9e367-921c-5703-b5c8-f4ef0ec283c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{x\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168092 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions are shown below:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (0,1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the derivative of the base inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions, we can differentiate combinations of these functions, by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of

$$
y = \arsech{(-x^2)}
$$

Using the formulas above together with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡(-{x}^{2})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-{x}^{2})\sqrt{1-{(-{x}^{2})}^{2}}}\cdot {(-{x}^{2})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{-{x}^{2}\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167021 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054812 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0cf33d77-f213-525d-99fb-8b9182428af7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0cf33d77-f213-525d-99fb-8b9182428af7" :question/id #uuid "0cf33d77-f213-525d-99fb-8b9182428af7" :question/math-academy-id "q-12244" :question/problem "Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ when $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Writing the radical as a rational exponent, we have

"Which statement correctly describes a **stable** equilibrium point?" :question/worked-solution "Let's recall the definitions of stability:

- An equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}$ is called *stable* if for any neighborhood $O$ of ${x}^{∗},$ there exists a neighborhood ${O}_{1}⊆O$ such that every orbit that begins inside ${O}_{1}$ at some point in time $t={t}_{0}$ remains inside $O$ for all $t>{t}_{0}.$

In plain words, this means that solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close, but may not converge to the equilibrium.

- An equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}$ is called *asymptotically stable* if it is stable and there exists a neighborhood $O$ of ${x}^{∗}$ such that every orbit that begins inside $O$ approaches ${x}^{∗}$ as $t\to \infty .$

In plain words, this means that solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close and converge to the equilibrium as $t\to \infty .$

- An equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}$ is called *unstable* if it is not stable.

In plain words, this means that solutions eventually move away from the equilibrium for some initial conditions arbitrarily close to it.

Therefore, the correct answer is the following:

Solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close, but do not necessarily converge to the equilibrium." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields Consider the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y,$ for which the conditional probability density function $f_{Y \,|\, X}(y \,|\, x)$ and the marginal density function $f_X(x)$ are shown above. Find the expression of the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for $0 \leq        x \leq        1, \: 0 \leq        y \leq        1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f_{Y \,|\, X}(y \,|\, x) =\dfrac{f(x, y)}{f_X (x)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- $f_X (x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

From the equation above, it follows that

$$
f(x,y) = f_{Y \,|\, X}(y \,|\, x) \cdot f_X (x).
$$

Now, for $0 \leq x \leq  1, \: 0 \leq y \leq  1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{3{x}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{3{x}^{2}+1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f_{Y \,|\, X}(y \,|\, x)$ equals $0.$ As a result, the product will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the joint probability density function is the following:
![](images/e5/e50432a004c16271fe9ffa680412a4729c9d03ce85c28d821d6b03585d2e24ba.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162114 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0309d911-015b-5e4c-9346-30c2d14fb0b7" "question-f873ff79-08e6-53a2-8403-85dc4a081919" "question-1967c2eb-a9e1-5379-9ffd-3708e127b5c8" "question-60bd267c-251c-5e47-b502-67f097fb7ef0" "question-3b02f20a-35d0-57b1-ada9-f1273f1f3904"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161680 :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:
![](images/5a/5ae264514c53b97339bfa9969057ed9462f183fc8a77658bd0615f0af148a67c.svg)

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function $f_{X \,|\, Y} (x \,|\, y)$ for $0 \leq             x \leq             1, \: 0 \leq             y \leq  1.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+y-0 \\  & =\frac{2y+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is the following:
![](images/27/27ba59d670061d91b96f80ee5400824993311d35c9edf7a887957936d74ace8c.svg)

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f_{X \,|\, Y} (x \,|\, y) = \dfrac{f(x, y)}{f_Y (y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0 \leq             x \leq             1, \: 0 \leq             y \leq  1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{(\frac{2y+1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{2y+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, $f_{X \,|\, Y}(x \,|\, y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:
![](images/24/242dc27ab006f389610d8f3bcd0297eed7d1809fb33b1b3b7c8b1f6b8dd532f7.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162113 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-05787bc3-261f-5b82-bb66-810cc0eb28ae" "question-d2c3b01f-8b1d-5c9b-95df-4bf4aec9fac1" "question-91a2a3a1-8ae1-5b13-976f-9bc558602e26" "question-a05be7fd-94f3-5604-ad03-bc6e74737579"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161679 :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

Find $P \left(Y <  \dfrac{1}{2} \,\bigg|\, X=1\right).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y \in A \,|\, X = x) = \int_A f_{Y \,|\, X} (y \,|\, x) \, \textrm{d}y,
$$

where $f_{Y \,|\, X} (y \,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function. 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}8{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =8{x}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =8{x}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}} \\  & =4{x}^{2}(\sqrt{x})^{2}-0 \\  & =4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is the following:

![](images/f5/f5bc55159d59fda4918d7da4c6dd26cab5600b086e0fe00846907b901b5d467e.svg)

Now recall that the conditional probability density function for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f_{Y \,|\, X} (y \,|\, x) =\dfrac{f(x, y)}{f_X (x)}
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- $f_X (x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<       x \leq       1, \: 0 \leq       y \leq       \sqrt{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{8{x}^{2}y}{4{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, $f_{Y \,|\, X} (y \,|\, x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

![](images/5a/5a3a34e2722798fa8b163ceb984302f300cd1d2fa6bc5fa5259e7451fceb6afc.svg)

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,X=1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=1)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2y}{1}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b3c1aae3-e457-548d-bfd0-11222eb5ea0e" :question/id #uuid "b3c1aae3-e457-548d-bfd0-11222eb5ea0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-143610" :question/problem "$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}5y\sqrt{x}, & 0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5x\sqrt{x}}{2}, & 0<x\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y,$ for which the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ and the marginal density function ${f}_{X}(x)$ are shown above. Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ for $0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{5y\sqrt{x}}{(\frac{5x\sqrt{x}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2x+y}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [4x+2] \\  & =\frac{2x+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+1}{2}, & \,0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{14}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ for $0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 3.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{14}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3x}{14}{\int }_{-1}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3x}{14}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{x}{14}\cdot [27-(-1)] \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x, & \,0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{14})}{2x} \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{28}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{28}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6ea5fec5-a0af-570b-bb41-e2eb4069b829"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6ea5fec5-a0af-570b-bb41-e2eb4069b829" :answer-field/id #uuid "6ea5fec5-a0af-570b-bb41-e2eb4069b829" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-849cc2b5-4f4e-50d8-9169-5a909d23bf4a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-20f62924-6dd5-52ac-bd28-479c20aca94e" "answer-ed3bcf1a-3dc4-5e1f-8c31-d1add2e63f21" "answer-849cc2b5-4f4e-50d8-9169-5a909d23bf4a" "answer-75fd5efd-a360-53f9-9006-6a6a1d8e159f" "answer-d03e8f09-0450-5bd4-8ebb-657acd93cbc9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20f62924-6dd5-52ac-bd28-479c20aca94e" :answer/id #uuid "20f62924-6dd5-52ac-bd28-479c20aca94e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "15y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ed3bcf1a-3dc4-5e1f-8c31-d1add2e63f21" :answer/id #uuid "ed3bcf1a-3dc4-5e1f-8c31-d1add2e63f21" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "21{y}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-849cc2b5-4f4e-50d8-9169-5a909d23bf4a" :answer/id #uuid "849cc2b5-4f4e-50d8-9169-5a909d23bf4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3{y}^{2}}{28}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-75fd5efd-a360-53f9-9006-6a6a1d8e159f" :answer/id #uuid "75fd5efd-a360-53f9-9006-6a6a1d8e159f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9{y}^{3}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d03e8f09-0450-5bd4-8ebb-657acd93cbc9" :answer/id #uuid "d03e8f09-0450-5bd4-8ebb-657acd93cbc9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{y}{14}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1967c2eb-a9e1-5379-9ffd-3708e127b5c8" :question/id #uuid "1967c2eb-a9e1-5379-9ffd-3708e127b5c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-143637" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$

$$

where

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{e}^{x+y}}{2})}{(\frac{{e}^{x}}{2})} \\  & ={e}^{y}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}+2y}{12}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{12}+\frac{y}{6})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{36}+\frac{xy}{6}]}_{x=0}^{x=3} \\  & =\frac{27}{36}+\frac{3y}{6}-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{y}{2} \\  & =\frac{2y+3}{4}.\end{aligned}

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2y+3}{4}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{2}+2y}{12})}{(\frac{2y+3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+2y}{3(2y+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

$$

Find $P(\frac{1}{4}<X<Y\,|\,Y=\frac{3}{4}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<X<Y\,|\,Y=\frac{3}{4}) & ={\int }_{1/4}^{y}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y=\frac{3}{4})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{3/4}\frac{(2\cdot \frac{3}{4}+x)}{(4\cdot \frac{3}{4}+2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{1/4}^{3/4}(x+\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{3x}{2}]}_{1/4}^{3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[{x}^{2}+3x]_{1/4}^{3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+3(\frac{3}{4})-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}-3(\frac{1}{4})) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(\frac{9}{16}+\frac{9}{4}-\frac{1}{16}-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6064d30a-0a9e-55a1-8d02-c3cb038cef8f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-d2c3b01f-8b1d-5c9b-95df-4bf4aec9fac1" :question/id #uuid "d2c3b01f-8b1d-5c9b-95df-4bf4aec9fac1" :question/math-academy-id "q-143622" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}y\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find $P(\frac{1}{4}<Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{3}{4}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{4}y\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{x}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{x}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x<1,0<y<2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4}y\sqrt{x})}{(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}y, & \,0\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{3}{4}) & =P(\frac{1}{4}<Y<\frac{3}{4}\,|\,X=\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{3/4}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{3}{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{3/4}\frac{1}{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{1/4}^{3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{9}{16}-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e2ec7e2d-e700-5713-ba66-48bf13c5d6e2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e2ec7e2d-e700-5713-ba66-48bf13c5d6e2" :answer-field/id #uuid "e2ec7e2d-e700-5713-ba66-48bf13c5d6e2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-bbc4d93c-b651-5691-9445-a738e7a4241d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a929b9b7-76e2-511c-af43-a8af03c8efa4" "answer-28a6421c-8bb1-5e74-b5ce-4488dab6060e" "answer-bbc4d93c-b651-5691-9445-a738e7a4241d" "answer-93edd067-6d4d-5723-af3e-e6c5a01044b8" "answer-b9f0f68c-757f-5ea6-b804-da070251f3d9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a929b9b7-76e2-511c-af43-a8af03c8efa4" :answer/id #uuid "a929b9b7-76e2-511c-af43-a8af03c8efa4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28a6421c-8bb1-5e74-b5ce-4488dab6060e" :answer/id #uuid "28a6421c-8bb1-5e74-b5ce-4488dab6060e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bbc4d93c-b651-5691-9445-a738e7a4241d" :answer/id #uuid "bbc4d93c-b651-5691-9445-a738e7a4241d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93edd067-6d4d-5723-af3e-e6c5a01044b8" :answer/id #uuid "93edd067-6d4d-5723-af3e-e6c5a01044b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9f0f68c-757f-5ea6-b804-da070251f3d9" :answer/id #uuid "b9f0f68c-757f-5ea6-b804-da070251f3d9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-91a2a3a1-8ae1-5b13-976f-9bc558602e26" :question/id #uuid "91a2a3a1-8ae1-5b13-976f-9bc558602e26" :question/math-academy-id "q-143619" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}3x, & \,y<x<1\,,\,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find $P(\frac{1}{4}<X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{6}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(X\in A\,|\,Y=y)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$  

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{y}^{1}3x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(1-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}(1-{y}^{2}), & \,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $y<x<1\,,\,0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{3x}{(\frac{3}{2}(1-{y}^{2}))} \\  & =\frac{2x}{1-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{1-{y}^{2}}, & \,0<y<x<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{6}) & =P(\frac{1}{4}<X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y=\frac{1}{6})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1}\frac{2x}{(1-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2})}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1}\frac{2x}{(\frac{35}{36})}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{36}{35}{\int }_{1/4}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{36}{35}{[{x}^{2}]}_{1/4}^{1} \\  & =\frac{36}{35}(1-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{27}{28}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7c446274-85cc-56ab-805a-72556fc77fd7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "q-143620" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e7448890-beaa-51f5-b2f0-83828889fb49"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e7448890-beaa-51f5-b2f0-83828889fb49" :answer-field/id #uuid "e7448890-beaa-51f5-b2f0-83828889fb49" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a0f9475b-b7d3-5932-90b4-6269e7ee9da9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d5b6de00-aaa3-58b8-919b-6ae993100929" "answer-8ccaa219-a0ea-583d-9e0c-efdebeabb3e6" "answer-a0f9475b-b7d3-5932-90b4-6269e7ee9da9" "answer-52c36d35-dfd3-59ca-b51c-6f8f7df4b4c3" "answer-30be591d-18e4-56ca-bd11-2cb0e73aa66b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d5b6de00-aaa3-58b8-919b-6ae993100929" :answer/id #uuid "d5b6de00-aaa3-58b8-919b-6ae993100929" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ccaa219-a0ea-583d-9e0c-efdebeabb3e6" :answer/id #uuid "8ccaa219-a0ea-583d-9e0c-efdebeabb3e6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0f9475b-b7d3-5932-90b4-6269e7ee9da9" :answer/id #uuid "a0f9475b-b7d3-5932-90b4-6269e7ee9da9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{24}{25}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52c36d35-dfd3-59ca-b51c-6f8f7df4b4c3" :answer/id #uuid "52c36d35-dfd3-59ca-b51c-6f8f7df4b4c3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-30be591d-18e4-56ca-bd11-2cb0e73aa66b" :answer/id #uuid "30be591d-18e4-56ca-bd11-2cb0e73aa66b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{25}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163291 :tutorial/content "We can easily extend the notion of conditional probability distributions for discrete random variables to continuous random variables.

For continuous random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the **conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y = y$** is given by

$$
f_{X|Y} (x|y) =\dfrac{f(x, y)}{f_Y (y)}, \qquad f_Y(y) \neq 0,
$$

and the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is given by

$$
f_{Y|X} (y|x) =\dfrac{f(x, y)}{f_X (x)}, \qquad f_X(x) \neq 0.
$$

Notice that these definitions are analogous to those for discrete random variables.

To compute probabilities, we work directly with these conditional PDFs. For example, to calculate the **conditional probability of $X$ given $Y,$** we use

$$
P(X \in A|Y = y) =\int_A f_{X|Y} (x|y)\, \textrm dx.
$$

In general, the conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ does not equal the conditional distribution of $Y$  given $X$. That is

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)  \ne f_{Y|X}(y|x).
$$

Finally, if $X$  and $Y$  are independent, then

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x),\qquad f_{Y|X}(y|x)=f_Y(y).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162176 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083325 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e64f0682-cd52-5135-b0b3-08e76e7a1873" "question-d6b501ec-18d5-51e8-9a88-2c1c73e44bb9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e64f0682-cd52-5135-b0b3-08e76e7a1873" :question/id #uuid "e64f0682-cd52-5135-b0b3-08e76e7a1873" :question/math-academy-id "q-95082" :question/problem "A group of students took a test and got an average score of $79.$ Also, $15%$ of the students scored lower than $66.$ Assuming that the scores of the students are normally distributed, find the standard deviation of their scores, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the grade obtained by a student. Then we have $X∼N(79,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 66)=0.15.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 66) & =0.15 \\ P(Z\le \frac{66-79}{\sigma }) & =0.15 \\ Φ(-\frac{13}{\sigma }) & =0.15 \\ -\frac{13}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.15).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.85)=1.0364,
$$

and therefore by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(1-0.85)={Φ}^{-1}(0.15)=-1.0364.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{13}{\sigma } & =-1.0364 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{-13}{-1.0364} \\  & ≈12.54.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c153adbb-ebdd-563f-aa07-ecead9219cce"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-217980d1-12ff-5532-90b2-461f43899f04" :question/id #uuid "217980d1-12ff-5532-90b2-461f43899f04" :question/math-academy-id "q-95091" :question/problem "A truck travels an average distance of $21\,\text{mi}$ with a gallon of gas. However, $15%$ of the time, a truck travels more than $26\,\text{mi}$ on a gallon of gas. Assuming that the distance the truck can travel with a gallon of gas is normally distributed, find, as a percent, the proportion of journeys that the truck travels less than $15\,\text{mi}$ on a gallon of gas. Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |

$$

$$

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.

| $z$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.3\,$ | $\,0.0918\,$ | $\,0.0901\,$ | $\,0.0885\,$ |
| $\,-1.2\,$ | $\,0.1093\,$ | $\,0.1075\,$ | $\,0.1056\,$ |
| $\,-1.1\,$ | $\,0.1292\,$ | $\,0.1271\,$ | $\,0.1251\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the distance traveled by the truck with a gallon of gas. Then we have $X∼N(21,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X\le 15).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>26)=0.15.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 26) & =1-P(X>26) \\  & =1-0.15 \\  & =0.85\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 26) & =0.85 \\ P(Z\le \frac{26-21}{\sigma }) & =0.85 \\ Φ(\frac{5}{\sigma }) & =0.85 \\ \frac{5}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.85)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.85)≈1.0364.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sigma } & =1.0364 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.2073 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.2073} \\  & ≈4.8239.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X\le 15)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 15) & =P(Z\le \frac{15-21}{4.8239}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -1.24) \\  & =Φ(-1.24) \\  & =0.1075 \\  & ≈10.8%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $10.8%$ of the time, a gallon of gas travels only $15\,\text{mi}$ or less." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields "d34b6be0-737c-5c5c-907f-c713ce8e6b32" :question/math-academy-id "q-133236" :question/problem "The average height of a player in a particular professional basketball league is $78$ inches. Additionally, $15%$ of players are over $82$ inches tall. Assuming that a player's height is normally distributed, find the percentage of players over $75$ inches tall, rounded to $1$ decimal place.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |

$$

$$

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.

| $z$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1660\,$ | $\,0.1635\,$ | $\,0.1611\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.1922\,$ | $\,0.1894\,$ | $\,0.1867\,$ |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2206\,$ | $\,0.2177\,$ | $\,0.2148\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the height of a randomly selected player. Then we have $X∼N(78,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>75).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>82)=0.15.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 82) & =1-P(X>82) \\  & =1-0.15 \\  & =0.85\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 82) & =0.85 \\ P(Z\le \frac{82-78}{\sigma }) & =0.85 \\ Φ(\frac{4}{\sigma }) & =0.85 \\ \frac{4}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.85)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.85)≈1.0364.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\sigma } & =1.0364 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.2591 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.2591} \\  & ≈3.85951.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X>75)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>75) & =1-P(X\le 75) \\  & =1-P(Z\le \frac{75-78}{3.85951}) \\  & ≈1-P(Z\le -0.78) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.78) \\  & =1-0.2177 \\  & =0.7823 \\  & ≈78.2%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $78.2%$ of players are over $75$ inch tall." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3d8d7f1f-3c0d-5b85-87f8-4a2364ded62c"] lifespan of LED light bulbs is normally distributed with a mean of $40,000$ hours and an unknown standard deviation $\sigma .$ Tests show that $10%$ of bulbs fail before $36,000$ hours. Assuming a normal model, find the standard deviation, **rounded to the nearest integer.**

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

$h$" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the lifespan of an LED bulb. Then we have $X∼N(40,000,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X<36,000)=0.10.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<36,000) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le \frac{36,000-40,000}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ Φ(-\frac{4,000}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ -\frac{4,000}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.9)=1.2816,
$$

and therefore, by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.10)=-1.2816.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{4,000}{\sigma } & =-1.2816 \\ \frac{4,000}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{4,000}{1.2816} \\ \sigma  & ≈3,121\,\text{h.}\end{aligned}

[:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078181 :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $3$ and the common difference is $2.$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
a_n= a_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

We are told that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}3}$ and the common difference is $d={\color{red}2}.$ So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\eqalign{
		a_n	&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
			&= {\color{blue}3} + (n - 1)({\color{red}2})  \[3pt]
			&= 3 + 2n -2 \[3pt]
			& =2n+1
}
$$

Therefore the formula for the $n$th term is $a_n = 2n+1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078464 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8eb6a381-be92-55fb-a425-16a442e609ca" "question-f4a1a68f-984f-511a-88be-72b335a1e5eb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078182 :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $0$ and the second term is $-2.$ Express your answer in function notation." :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)= f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

We are given the first term $f(1)={\color{blue}0}.$ Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as

$$
d=-2 - 0 = {\color{red}-2}.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\eqalign{
f(n)&= f(1)+(n-1)d \[3pt]
&= {\color{blue}0} + (n - 1)({\color{red}-2})  \[3pt]
&= 0 - 2n + 2 \[3pt]
&= 2 - 2n
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is $f(n) = 2 - 2n.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078465 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c129ef1c-2ac1-51e8-b05a-e3f368cf0b6f" "question-013f16dc-6316-5e58-8d55-c6702c89f1f0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078184 :question/problem "Find the $50$th term of the following arithmetic sequence.

$$
-5, \: -8, \: -11, \: \ldots
$$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
a_n= a_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
{\color{blue}-5}, \: -8, \: -11, \ldots,
$$

we see that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}-5}$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=-8-(-5)={\color{red}-3}.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
&= {\color{blue}-5} + (n - 1)({\color{red}-3})  \[3pt]
& =-5 -3n + 3 \[3pt]
&=-3n-2
}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $50$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=50\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
a_n &=-3n-2 \[7pt]
a_{50} &= -3(50)-2 \[3pt]
&= -150-2 \[3pt]
&= -152	
}
$$

Therefore, the $50$th term of the sequence is $a_{50}=-152.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078466 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-59d1d85b-3b0d-5f71-98d3-9151bc5e371c" "question-36a772ef-4e2c-580e-97bd-8718ab74d591"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078186 :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of the arithmetic sequence that has a $7$th term equal to $-34$ and a common difference of $-5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $a_{7}=-34$ is $6$ jumps after $a_1$.

![](images/ea/ea803977d4861ad654bd29ff15f706fdd1d11f71dbf7c885f175fe8168f21b66.png)

Hence, we can write

$$
a_{7} = a_1 + 6d,
$$

and solve for $a_1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{7} & ={a}_{1}+6d \\ -34 & ={a}_{1}+6(-5) \\ -34 & ={a}_{1}-30 \\ -4 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-4+(n-1)(-5) \\  & =-4-5n+5 \\  & =1-5n.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-9b2690e5-910c-5f9f-9900-ab879a8e0507" :question/id #uuid "9b2690e5-910c-5f9f-9900-ab879a8e0507" :question/math-academy-id "q-5288" :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $5$ and the common difference is $1.$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

We are told that the first term is ${a}_{1}=5$ and the common difference is $d=1.$ So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =5+(n-1)(1) \\  & =5+n-1 \\  & =4+n\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $d$ is a common difference.

To illustrate how this works, suppose we want to find the $20$th term of the following arithmetic sequence:

$$
{\color{blue}2}, \: 5, \: 8, \: 11, \: 14, \: \ldots
$$

The first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2},$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=5-2={\color{red}3}.
$$

So, we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =2+(n-1)(3) \\  & =2+3n-3 \\  & =3n-1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $20$th term, we can use this formula with $n=20\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =3n-1 \\ {a}_{20} & =3(20)-1 \\  & =60-1 \\  & =59\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $20$th term is $a_{20}=59.$ Using the formula was much quicker than writing out all $20$ terms of the sequence!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078684 Therefore, the common difference is $d=-2.25.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c6014564-1e53-5cb5-8d8c-c8d21f1fe08e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c6014564-1e53-5cb5-8d8c-c8d21f1fe08e" :answer-field/id #uuid "c6014564-1e53-5cb5-8d8c-c8d21f1fe08e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-aaf6f79d-d6ee-5f05-a6e5-f7bf8776711a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-aaf6f79d-d6ee-5f05-a6e5-f7bf8776711a" "answer-e8157d94-5b61-5154-8e4e-d4a4ee2c3a4b" "answer-488a956f-9bc7-5837-8db3-c481d1b56fc8" "answer-6bced045-23f8-5104-9d2d-7d8e3acb682e" "answer-84168e80-8a3b-5417-900e-1ead231a2125"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aaf6f79d-d6ee-5f05-a6e5-f7bf8776711a" :answer/id #uuid "aaf6f79d-d6ee-5f05-a6e5-f7bf8776711a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e8157d94-5b61-5154-8e4e-d4a4ee2c3a4b" :answer/id #uuid "e8157d94-5b61-5154-8e4e-d4a4ee2c3a4b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-488a956f-9bc7-5837-8db3-c481d1b56fc8" :answer/id #uuid "488a956f-9bc7-5837-8db3-c481d1b56fc8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6bced045-23f8-5104-9d2d-7d8e3acb682e" :answer/id #uuid "6bced045-23f8-5104-9d2d-7d8e3acb682e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84168e80-8a3b-5417-900e-1ead231a2125" :answer/id #uuid "84168e80-8a3b-5417-900e-1ead231a2125" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079728 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the fourth term of an arithmetic sequence is $6$ and the fifth term is $12.$ Can we use this information to compute the common difference of the sequence?

The first thing to note is that the sequence is *increasing*, and therefore we expect the common difference $d$ to be positive.

Now, let's take a look at the jumps:

![](images/6b/6b82ba58c986aa32635e2ebbd8b1e0fd0affdbc81e35a015960777fa72d5f72b.png)

Because $a_4 = 6$ and $a_5 = 12$ are **consecutive terms**, meaning that $a_5$ comes straight after $a_4$ in the sequence, we can easily compute the common difference $d$ by subtracting $a_4$ from $a_5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{5}-{a}_{4} \\  & =12-6 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079729 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the second and fifth terms only of an arithmetic sequence. For example, suppose that we know that

$$
a_2 = {\color{red}8}, \quad a_5 = {\color{red}23}
$$

These terms are not consecutive, and so how can we figure out the common difference $d?$

First, let's take a look at the jumps:

![](images/ff/ff83c75935acca7ddd5c421cd81fad85685c68fd782d1d832c068237c751753d.png)

We see that between ${\color{red}8}$ and ${\color{red}23}$, there are a total of ${\color{blue}3}$ jumps. So, to find the value of a single jump, we can take the total difference and divide it by the number of jumps:

$$
d = \frac{{\color{red}23}\,-\,{\color{red}8}}{\color{blue}3} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5
$$

We can check that our result $d=5$ is correct by using it to figure out the intermediate terms. Indeed, the common difference $d=5$ gets us from $a_2={\color{red}8}$ to $a_5={\color{red}23}$ in ${\color{blue}3}$ jumps:

![](images/7a/7aa192675aeb3c7be78617035b74362b38974e8501d95c0692238811ae4769f1.png)

In general, if we're given two terms $a_n$ and $a_m$ of an arithmetic sequence, then we can calculate the common difference using the following formula:

$$
d = \frac{a_n-a_m}{n-m}
$$

Using this formula to calculate the common difference between $a_{2}=8$ and $a_{5}=23,$ we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{5}-{a}_{2}}{5-2} \\  & =\frac{23-8}{5-2} \\  & =\frac{15}{3} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078685 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186171297 :answer-field/choices 17592186171298] [:db/retract 17592186171297 :answer-field/choices 17592186171299] [:db/retract 17592186171297 :answer-field/choices 17592186171300] [:db/retract 17592186171297 :answer-field/choices 17592186171301] [:db/retract 17592186171297 :answer-field/choices 17592186171302] {:db/id 17592186172612 :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ -3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186171297 :answer-field/correct "answer-7ae566ac-fe5f-5c58-a6f9-26a40344d78b" :answer-field/choices
