$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{t}^{2}+t-6}{{t}^{2}-9t+14} & =\frac{(t+3)(t-2)}{(t-2)(t-7)} \\  & =\frac{t+3}{t-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{{t}^{2}+t-6}{{t}^{2}-9t+14} & ={lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{t+3}{t-7} \\  & =\frac{2+3}{2-7} \\  & =\frac{5}{(-5)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}-16}{{y}^{2}-4y} & =\frac{(y-4)(y+4)}{y(y-4)} \\  & =\frac{y+4}{y}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{5}+5{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(3{x}^{2}+5x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}(3{x}^{2}+5x-2) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}(3x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 480} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186074645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075006 :tutorial/content "A **polynomial equation** is an equation that can be written in the form

$$
P_n(x)=0,
$$

where $P_n(x)$  is a polynomial of degree $n.$
A **cubic equation** is a polynomial equation of degree $n=3.$

To solve a polynomial equation with no constant term, we factor the polynomial part using the greatest common factor.
Once we've done that, we can apply the zero product rule to the resulting factors.

For instance, consider the cubic equation $x^3-x=0.$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $x^2-1$ using the difference of squares formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x+1)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, we conclude that the solutions are ${\color{red}x=0},$ ${\color{blue}x = -1},$ and ${\color{purple}x=1}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+50{y}^{2}+100y & =5{y}^{2}+25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+100y & =25y \\ 6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3y.$ We can factor out the $3y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0 \\ 3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+15y+25$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0 \\ 3y(2y+5)(y+5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3} \\ 5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-8x+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0 \\ 5x(x-1)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=7.$"} :step/id #uuid "33189ef3-2537-5d6d-bc82-5263f6083b68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496384}} {:db/id 17592186496359 :step/content {:db/id 17592186496320 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "296694e3-5319-547a-8c8f-0fc26e3a8b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-2,\,-3,\,5" :db/id 17592186495601} {:answer/id #uuid "4658aaeb-11d9-5b92-a7a2-aea2864fd98a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-2,\,0,\,5" :db/id 17592186495668} {:answer/id #uuid "4a808032-3416-51f3-bad1-93a62d09b580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-3,\,0,\,5" :db/id 17592186495681} {:answer/id #uuid "ab32c019-df2f-511a-adec-83c31e26c5c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-3,\,0,\,2" :db/id 17592186495894} {:answer/id #uuid "de7814e7-b746-525b-9bf4-f606ff9e5397" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-2,\,0,\,3" :db/id 17592186496001}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495668} :answer-field/id #uuid "498bf339-9275-5f3a-b0a2-353256e90566" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496111}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e5110c54-de9e-5958-ac4d-933027f79b9c" :question/math-academy-id "q-3977" :question/problem "If ${z}^{3}-5{z}^{2}=-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z$, then $z=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |

If $F(x,y)$ is the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y,$ find $F\left(2,1\right).$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y) = \sum\limits_{x_i \leq x} \sum\limits_{y_i \leq y} f(x_i, y_i).
$$

By definition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2,1) & =P(X\le 2,Y\le 1).\end{aligned}
$$

We start by highlighting all cells in the table that correspond to $X \leq 2, Y \leq 1.$

| $f$ | $Y=-2$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2,1) & ={\sum }_{x\le 2}{\sum }_{y\le 1}f(x,y) \\  & =f(1,-2)+f(1,-1)+f(1,0) \\  & =0.1+0.3+0.05 \\  & =0.45.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048800} {:db/id 17592186050256} {:db/id 17592186051001} {:db/id 17592186162411 :question/id #uuid "579f1fda-9534-54f2-9a64-f554fdec8e40" :question/math-academy-id "q-145559" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162124 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f3c48f82-c3ed-5014-b1f5-cd9e8de542f0" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Joint CDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "863b10fe-f745-5566-ae64-5eb30b06c2a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186159669} {:answer/id #uuid "8a944662-c5dd-5606-9c9f-6709fa172b0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1" :db/id 17592186159670} {:answer/id #uuid "a76f7163-9ca0-5f82-af73-cb015fc87e68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.35" :db/id 17592186159671} {:answer/id #uuid "c622b1a2-e96f-5222-bc89-4198a6a07bb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.55" :db/id 17592186159672} {:answer/id #uuid "21f58f58-8d2d-5c6a-901a-783e42784a72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.15" :db/id 17592186159673}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c622b1a2-e96f-5222-bc89-4198a6a07bb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.55" :db/id 17592186159672} :answer-field/id #uuid "f03c2b00-d99f-52aa-a91b-33654f63b2f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186159668}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown below.

If $F(x,y)$ is the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y,$ find $F(2,4).$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

By definition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2,4) & =P(X\le 2,Y\le 4).\end{aligned}
$$

We start by highlighting all cells in the table that correspond to $X\le 2,Y\le 4.$

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |

Therefore, we obtain

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(9,10)=0.65,\,F(6,10)=0.31,\,F(3,10)=0.12,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{3,6,9,12\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Find $P(3<X\le 9,Y\le 10).$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/77/7790a013e37bb86c00b44b1c022d6597f9bbdd57616c48e7ee7dfe8ddf512c63.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/37/379f0690fdbe92b7fb8f66cce4f12b214a23c6299fb8df71edf56d37fc0387fe.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(9,10)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,10)$ (the red region below).

![](images/90/90a6730747b59a9886acbdf21880ca6a7ec3266142522ea5b32f07090963a98d.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<X\le 9,Y\le 10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 10)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(3,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 10)}} \\  & =F(9,10)-F(3,10) \\  & =0.65-0.12 \\  & =0.53.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481349 :question/id #uuid "1374041d-2f69-55e3-9b42-ce863bb1bab0" :question/math-academy-id "q-146615" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162125 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "02f8da68-ea1e-5f20-8f1a-7a38508e1f1f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Cumulative Probabilities Given Values From the Joint CDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05a1a33d-ed6a-57ac-b7c7-d80e7811473a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.34" :db/id 17592186480748} {:answer/id #uuid "85b516c6-df16-5177-b323-6e0f55271ea3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.43" :db/id 17592186480997} {:answer/id #uuid "e248ad4f-2ddb-5621-a2c5-b027b720eeff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.61" :db/id 17592186481166} {:answer/id #uuid "ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.52" :db/id 17592186481190} {:answer/id #uuid "fe0f133d-d936-51dc-8dad-167e59ac346b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.09" :db/id 17592186481231}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ea93ddf2-c74d-5131-8f0c-698558bc1ccd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.52" :db/id 17592186481190} :answer-field/id #uuid "0973e0ae-8949-52fe-9d14-7a1a4925ba53" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186481242}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(4,1)=0.77,\,F(4,-1)=0.15,\,F(1,1)=0.19,\,F(1,-1)=0.09,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/01/01e04dfdac5f4abc16bd856dcfbe1b7361010cce2e7779658a33f293c1c52ae4.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/2d/2d2525118ca3b62c0829c0308fab168d0b806dfa13302c007a63cd354314d63f.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(1,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X\le 4,-1<Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le -1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(4,1)-F(4,-1)-F(1,1)+F(1,-1) \\  & =0.77-0.15-0.19+0.09 \\  & =0.52.\end{aligned}

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(4,3)=0.8,\,F(1,3)=0,\,F(4,1)=0.3,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{2,4,6\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{0,1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Find $P(X\le 4,1<Y\le 3).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6\}\times \{0,1,2,3,4\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/2b/2b159f4ba1873270f42b7afd2fdc4b969672c7d3cb7e694d519ab82dab33b283.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/e1/e186cf0e38e938798cdcd5bc10a5334230cc78cc77d114a14eba0c07702a1cdc.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained by taking all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,3)$ (the blue region below) and *subtracting* all points in the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1)$ (the red region below).

![](images/eb/ebcfd8e0b553cab38a76eac77aab45186db92b3fe47a1fbb87a8623db4c29389.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 4,1<Y\le 3) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,3)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 3)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & =F(4,3)-F(4,1) \\  & =0.8-0.3 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481406 :question/id #uuid "af981bc5-9b24-55d4-b993-5b515801ef39" :question/math-academy-id "q-146626"} {:db/id 17592186481437 :question/id #uuid "fab237a1-fe76-5f6d-bb1c-9924690227b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-146620" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162125 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "02f8da68-ea1e-5f20-8f1a-7a38508e1f1f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Cumulative Probabilities Given Values From the Joint CDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e0814a4-0dea-5ca4-b7fc-9b692b925da5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.6" :db/id 17592186480860} {:answer/id #uuid "b285d0a5-dff5-5f04-93cf-71561d9480cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.22" :db/id 17592186481075} {:answer/id #uuid "d9741b9a-5671-58f6-b927-57967f816283" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.7" :db/id 17592186481145} {:answer/id #uuid "e8bf43fa-0a43-5b86-8a6b-461dae770a69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.12" :db/id 17592186481183} {:answer/id #uuid "f19b40dc-ac21-5cf6-a61d-ef12a77f06e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.48" :db/id 17592186481209}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f19b40dc-ac21-5cf6-a61d-ef12a77f06e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.48" :db/id 17592186481209} :answer-field/id #uuid "d52b8610-a26d-566a-a9f0-2b005b0ef722" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186481318}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $P(6<X\le 9,4<Y\le 10).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/77/7790a013e37bb86c00b44b1c022d6597f9bbdd57616c48e7ee7dfe8ddf512c63.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/65/6535c5bf152e8a9b09bf5522cdc442668add6c4cc7a0df4e07307f9931886a80.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(9,10).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(9,4)$ and $(6,10).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(6,4).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6<X\le 9,4<Y\le 10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 4)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 4)}} \\  & =F(9,10)-F(9,4)-F(6,10)+F(6,4) \\  & =0.8-0.3-0.4+0.2 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}

$$
{S}_{X}=\{0,1\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x>1,y>6.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(7,1)=\frac{9}{16},\,F(7,-2)=\frac{1}{4},\,F(3,1)=\frac{1}{8},\,F(3,-2)=\frac{1}{16},
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{1,3,5,7,9\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(5\le X\le 8,-1\le Y\le 1).$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,3,5,7,9\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/9e/9ebff161899c6f61af3dffc1a5a0069de14bafd9b138293a945138e2951d066d.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(7,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(3,-2)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/e2/e25278ed6d9712d8d2d2cabda5d1d0dbbf10aa8193f1342e7b4b66b26f9154e3.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(7,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(7,-2)$ and $(3,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,-2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5\le X\le 8,-1\le Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(7,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{bottom-right corner at }(7,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-left corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{bottom-left corner at }(3,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(7,1)-F(7,-2)-F(3,1)+F(3,-2) \\  & =\frac{9}{16}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481341 :question/id #uuid "01cad121-bd37-5572-936b-c4e7143fa3ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-146843"} {:db/id 17592186481393 :question/id #uuid "8dece31e-c114-5d98-b9c8-904ef5ba8d5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-146851" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b97d9a7a-fa12-5d8d-8958-39625f117979" :knowledge-point/title "Further Finding Cumulative Probabilities Given Values From the Joint CDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58bac764-44f8-55c1-ba07-ab0f55dee029" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.05" :db/id 17592186480900} {:answer/id #uuid "afcef1f2-ba8a-55d4-b054-349a510940db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.23" :db/id 17592186481070} {:answer/id #uuid "b6cfd97d-9e66-5650-8d9b-e6f83d8cc114" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1" :db/id 17592186481087} {:answer/id #uuid "d5817d11-103f-57c6-b7df-8777bf2f338b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.32" :db/id 17592186481136} {:answer/id #uuid "e32a7cb9-b939-581c-bc82-d395bf018748" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.28" :db/id 17592186481169}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b6cfd97d-9e66-5650-8d9b-e6f83d8cc114" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1" :db/id 17592186481087} :answer-field/id #uuid "ad0272b4-dd5a-544a-a7d4-a49f4c49e16a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186481299}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(1,1)=0.7,\,F(1,-2)=0.3,\,F(-2,1)=0.4,\,F(-2,-2)=0.1,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(-1.5\le X\le 1.5,-1.5\le Y\le 1.5).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/ae/ae7d480e52257825e679349ce185b4aa08ed3b096fd7a780ece56c90439798fe.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(1,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(-2,-2)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/5b/5bcb1b0b518485dfcd4066a0259fea4a2dc050be47e95b4de0b925d8f1c997aa.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(1,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(1,-2)$ and $(-2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(-2,-2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.5\le X\le 1.5,-1.5\le Y\le 1.5) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(1,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 1,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(-2,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le -2,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(1,1)-F(1,-2)-F(-2,1)+F(-2,-2) \\  & =0.7-0.3-0.4+0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481438 :question/id #uuid "fd922824-164f-5af2-954c-b939958ff429" :question/math-academy-id "q-146845" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b97d9a7a-fa12-5d8d-8958-39625f117979" :knowledge-point/title "Further Finding Cumulative Probabilities Given Values From the Joint CDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04ed47b4-e775-566f-bc2c-56a2a7bded91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.23" :db/id 17592186480745} {:answer/id #uuid "7d933f6f-e2c3-51e2-80f4-1f904b3bbf7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.086" :db/id 17592186480973} {:answer/id #uuid "9d89dae4-9bbc-5113-9c23-1d88b96505c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.47" :db/id 17592186481042} {:answer/id #uuid "be91de9f-ef83-54e9-8ed1-7d56afbe15c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.63" :db/id 17592186481103} {:answer/id #uuid "e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.24" :db/id 17592186481161}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e0f16e58-ba50-5519-b0c9-2c7d1935a069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.24" :db/id 17592186481161} :answer-field/id #uuid "7b5302b1-965f-57a3-8e52-58216fd37b2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186481280}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. - The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3004} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163101 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163341 :tutorial/content "The **joint cumulative distribution function** (or joint CDF) of two discrete random variables $X,$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
F(x,y) = P( X \leq x, Y \leq y)  = \sum\limits_{x_i \leq x} \sum\limits_{y_i \leq y} f(x_i, y_i).
$$

The sets $S_X$ and $S_Y,$ on which the variables $X$ and $Y$ are defined, are the **supports** of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

We can see from this definition that the joint CDF is analogous to the cumulative distribution function of a single random variable.

Consider the joint PMF for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

Here, the supports of $X$ and $Y$ are $S_X = \{ 0, 1 \}$ and $S_Y = \{ 0, 1, 2 \},$ respectively. 

As an example, let's compute $F(1,1).$ By definition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1,1) & =P(X\le 1,Y\le 1).\end{aligned}
$$

We start by highlighting all cells in the table that correspond to $X \leq 1, Y \leq 1.$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1,1) & =f(0,0)+f(0,1)+f(1,0)+f(1,1) \\  & =0.1+0.2+0.3+0.2 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68282cd4-eb49-54e1-a97a-8d49988c8922" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6430 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "494e3329-5465-5724-b614-4ecacfaaed97" :step/math-academy-id 38939} {:db/id 17592186163152 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163360 :tutorial/content "Consider the joint PMF for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ |

We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\neq 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

![](images/c6/c6d8e4012a0a16f865bf229549512ff772e103d3fcd7667738cf7250d7267e84.png)

 

Now, the joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y) = \sum\limits_{x_i \leq x} \sum\limits_{y_i \leq y} f(x_i, y_i).
$$

Geometrically, then, the joint CDF gives the total "probability mass" that lies inside the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.

For example, consider the point $(2,1.5)$ and the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at this point, shown below.

![](images/46/46837da3e8f8f44831da4e6b464e9f8562f322b17f584df3fc87912d1c09d4c4.png)

The value of $F(2,1.5)$ equals the total "probability mass" contained within this rectangle. That is,

$$
F(2,1.5) = f(1,0) + f(2,0) + f(1,1) + f(2,1).
$$

It's worth highlighting a few important cases:

- If our rectangular region doesn't include any points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 0.$

![](images/bb/bb5faa2b42c9ece2fe80cff4dd27a8b720cb363f5319c3cb5f5dd065f818c403.png)

- If our rectangular region includes *all* points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 1.$

![](images/81/811b15e3cea46e0a4a546e68217a2994a7b2a7b80d6bc444bc6fbaa2ebaed355.png)

Finally, we note the following properties of the joint CDF:

- $0 \leq F(x,y) \leq 1$

- The marginal CDF of $X$ is given by $F_X(x) = F(x, \infty).$

- The marginal CDF of $Y$ is given by $F_Y(y) = F( \infty, y).$

- $F(\infty, \infty) = 1$

- $F(-\infty,y) = F(x, -\infty) = 0$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then $F(x,y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d6a285ac-6fdf-506c-9228-20857fedc5b3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6977 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Joint CDF"} :step/id #uuid "5d0f7f20-6219-5e6b-9d38-ad689f056506" :step/math-academy-id 42192 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163108}}] :activity/title "The Joint CDF of Two Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162165} {:db/id 17592186163101 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163341 :tutorial/content "The **joint cumulative distribution function** (or joint CDF) of two discrete random variables $X,$ and $Y$ is defined as

The value of $F(2,1.5)$ equals the total "probability mass" contained within this rectangle. That is,

$$
F(2,1.5) = f(1,0) + f(2,0) + f(1,1) + f(2,1).
$$

It's worth highlighting a few important cases:

- If our rectangular region doesn't include any points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 0.$

![](images/bb/bb5faa2b42c9ece2fe80cff4dd27a8b720cb363f5319c3cb5f5dd065f818c403.png)

- If our rectangular region includes *all* points where the probability is nonzero, then we must have $F(x,y) = 1.$

![](images/81/811b15e3cea46e0a4a546e68217a2994a7b2a7b80d6bc444bc6fbaa2ebaed355.png)

Finally, we note the following properties of the joint CDF:

- $0 \leq F(x,y) \leq 1$

- The marginal CDF of $X$ is given by $F_X(x) = F(x, \infty).$

- The marginal CDF of $Y$ is given by $F_Y(y) = F( \infty, y).$

- $F(\infty, \infty) = 1$

- $F(-\infty,y) = F(x, -\infty) = 0$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then $F(x,y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d6a285ac-6fdf-506c-9228-20857fedc5b3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6977 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Joint CDF"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186495222} :activity/id #uuid "8dcc3cb1-af1f-5fd5-a39e-26295bdafc56" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050971 :topic/id #uuid "767f9ccb-0c08-5d76-97c4-5882b4f99cd1" :topic/math-academy-id 3004} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186495195 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495160 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "213c512b-4d83-52c6-aea3-4aa799b73e2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186494383} {:answer/id #uuid "5226bb01-1d74-50d5-ae38-837109e0e401" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3" :db/id 17592186494481} {:answer/id #uuid "52c9b21a-4477-5890-bc16-7ba55dac052a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2" :db/id 17592186494483} {:answer/id #uuid "67f944a8-f948-5604-bc8c-ae5256daf681" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8" :db/id 17592186494524} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad4d637-0bcc-57fd-a92b-74aa8cebd839" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186494536}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494481} :answer-field/id #uuid "f1436435-7d0e-595c-99fd-60d4245df591" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495035}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9cd0722-c129-5c15-8f19-958d5be79276" :question/math-academy-id "q-146618" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(9,10)=0.8,\,F(9,4)=0.3,\,F(6,10)=0.4,\,F(6,4)=0.2,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{3,6,9,12\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Find $P(6<X\le 9,4<Y\le 10).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{3,6,9,12\}\times \{2,4,6,8,10,12\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support.

![](images/77/7790a013e37bb86c00b44b1c022d6597f9bbdd57616c48e7ee7dfe8ddf512c63.png)

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/65/6535c5bf152e8a9b09bf5522cdc442668add6c4cc7a0df4e07307f9931886a80.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(9,10).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(9,4)$ and $(6,10).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(6,4).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6<X\le 9,4<Y\le 10) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(9,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 9,Y\le 4)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,10)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 10)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(6,4)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 6,Y\le 4)}} \\  & =F(9,10)-F(9,4)-F(6,10)+F(6,4) \\  & =0.8-0.3-0.4+0.2 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2f96dcd0-a5cb-5224-89fd-80e1b854634b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495230}} {:db/id 17592186495199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495171 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54feaaa8-dd22-5ec0-9f20-e02541fd09ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{y}" :db/id 17592186494489} {:answer/id #uuid "8a615a1e-0c9e-52a7-9428-2729a456062a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186494628} {:answer/id #uuid "a9eb4b4d-0d8f-5334-bdd7-099229f155e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x" :db/id 17592186494710} {:answer/id #uuid "c50b7eba-5426-53e7-a693-b3a4082cd5dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186494779} {:answer/id #uuid "dc5a4b19-57de-5fe5-bab6-461309d9b799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186494839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494779} :answer-field/id #uuid "473ef6d8-60c9-5504-8ce5-d78f894c72f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494949}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fb06fe3b-f0e6-5f9b-9f03-e38285ba59c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-146415" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{-1,0,1\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3\}.
$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x<-1,y>2.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-1,0,1\}\times \{1,2,3\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x<-1$ and $y>2,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/41/41e8a9d9ec73c9c10a73c4dcd8a8fe9051401d6ab31c8274fdf8f22adb2437da.png)

Since every value in the support of $X$ is at least $-1$ and $x<-1,$ no possible value of $X$ satisfies $X\le x.$ Therefore, there are no points in the joint support that lie in the region $Δ.$

Hence,

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3c9389f8-aafc-528d-9a81-dbc2216f32cd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495195}} {:db/id 17592186495221 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f01c561e-5fd3-5431-aa89-b6c0a3ea800f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{32}" :db/id 17592186159729} {:answer/id #uuid "128c143c-1206-5a0d-92ce-dad3f6df6aa1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{16}" :db/id 17592186159730} {:answer/id #uuid "2cac8f41-fff7-5b34-ae38-570dd1faab05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186159731} {:answer/id #uuid "3396fd2c-6299-532f-81b0-89d0d78d2a17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{16}" :db/id 17592186159732} {:answer/id #uuid "72d5813b-32a6-53c1-b39a-47c432820dd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186159733}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186159733} :answer-field/id #uuid "1a2220de-b4ac-5e91-8f92-853a80a549e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186159728}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4909f9a0-a8a3-5a67-aa19-15cc754b3e1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-145909" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. $$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5\le X\le 8,-1\le Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(7,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{bottom-right corner at }(7,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-left corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{bottom-left corner at }(3,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(7,1)-F(7,-2)-F(3,1)+F(3,-2) \\  & =\frac{9}{16}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

{S}_{X}=\{1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(3\le X<5,0\le Y<2).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/62/6287f4884b335466bc7e1d6da17190f32d447f065e37a37e79a1aa48a6109415.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(4,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(2,-1)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/d4/d4d76ca2e80bccda9cbcfa4e28c628dffcec62b3fb42d62f9315fce2623e12fe.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$

$$
F(4,1)=0.8,\,F(4,-1)=0.2,\,F(2,1)=0.3,\,F(2,-1)=0.1,
$$

and the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{1,2,3,4,5\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Find $P(3\le X<5,0\le Y<2).$" :question/worked-solution "Note the following:

- For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/62/6287f4884b335466bc7e1d6da17190f32d447f065e37a37e79a1aa48a6109415.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(4,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(2,-1)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/d4/d4d76ca2e80bccda9cbcfa4e28c628dffcec62b3fb42d62f9315fce2623e12fe.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(4,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(4,-1)$ and $(2,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,-1).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X<4,-1\le Y<1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(4,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 4,Y\le -1)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,-1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le -1)}} \\  & =F(4,1)-F(4,-1)-F(2,1)+F(2,-1) \\  & =0.8-0.2-0.3+0.1 \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9c8530ec-4ccc-55e4-81ee-29272379bcc6"} {:db/id 17592186495199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495171 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54feaaa8-dd22-5ec0-9f20-e02541fd09ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{y}" :db/id 17592186494489} {:answer/id #uuid "8a615a1e-0c9e-52a7-9428-2729a456062a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186494628} {:answer/id #uuid "a9eb4b4d-0d8f-5334-bdd7-099229f155e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x" :db/id 17592186494710} {:answer/id #uuid "c50b7eba-5426-53e7-a693-b3a4082cd5dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186494779} {:answer/id #uuid "dc5a4b19-57de-5fe5-bab6-461309d9b799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186494839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494779} :answer-field/id #uuid "473ef6d8-60c9-5504-8ce5-d78f894c72f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494949}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fb06fe3b-f0e6-5f9b-9f03-e38285ba59c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-146415" :question/problem "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where the supports of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, are

$$
{S}_{X}=\{-1,0,1\},\,{S}_{Y}=\{1,2,3\}.
$$

Find an expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x<-1,y>2.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\sum }_{{x}_{i}\le x}{\sum }_{{y}_{i}\le y}f({x}_{i},{y}_{i}).
$$

Note the following:

- We can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{-1,0,1\}\times \{1,2,3\}.
$$

Let's sketch the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x<-1$ and $y>2,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/41/41e8a9d9ec73c9c10a73c4dcd8a8fe9051401d6ab31c8274fdf8f22adb2437da.png)

Since every value in the support of $X$ is at least $-1$ and $x<-1,$ no possible value of $X$ satisfies $X\le x.$ Therefore, there are no points in the joint support that lie in the region $Δ.$

Hence,

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3c9389f8-aafc-528d-9a81-dbc2216f32cd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495195}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "54feaaa8-dd22-5ec0-9f20-e02541fd09ca" :answer/type {:db/id - For a given joint PMF $f(x,y),$ we can think of each point where $f(x,y)\ne 0$ as a point mass in the plane, where the "probability mass" at each point equals the probability associated with that point.

- The joint CDF $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the total "probability mass" that lies in the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axis.

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}=\{1,3,5,7,9\}\times \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
$$

Let's plot the points in ${S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y},$ which contains the joint support, and sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/9e/9ebff161899c6f61af3dffc1a5a0069de14bafd9b138293a945138e2951d066d.png)

Notice that this region encompasses the same possible support points as the rectangular region with its top-right corner at $(7,1)$ and bottom-left corner at $(3,-2)$ below, where the top and right boundaries are inclusive and the bottom and left boundaries are exclusive.

![](images/e2/e25278ed6d9712d8d2d2cabda5d1d0dbbf10aa8193f1342e7b4b66b26f9154e3.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(7,1).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(7,-2)$ and $(3,1).$

3\. Finally, we need to add back the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(3,-2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5\le X\le 8,-1\le Y\le 1) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(7,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{bottom-right corner at }(7,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 7,Y\le -2)}}-\overset{\text{top-left corner at }(3,1)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le 1)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{bottom-left corner at }(3,-2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 3,Y\le -2)}} \\  & =F(7,1)-F(7,-2)-F(3,1)+F(3,-2) \\  & =\frac{9}{16}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8838afa5-73ed-52cd-9c3d-38413c09ae41" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495199}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f01c561e-5fd3-5431-aa89-b6c0a3ea800f" :answer/type {:db/id :step/content {:db/id 17592186079615 :tutorial/content "In general, the limit of a function $f(x)$ at a point only exists if *both* the left-sided and right-sided limits *exist* and are the *same*.

For example, suppose we want to compute $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)$ for the function whose graph is shown below. To do this, we must first compute the left and right-sided limits.

![](images/d9/d99cb9753d63d0812245159b6727e30408eb6cd89d01ecb2f4090f65925527f1.png)

As $x$ approaches $2$ from the left, $y$ approaches $0$. However, as $x$ approaches $2$ from the right, $y$ approaches $1$. Therefore, we have the following left and right-sided limits.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}Left-sided limit: & lim_(x → 2^{-})f(x) = 0 \\ Right-sided limit: & lim_(x → 2^{+})f(x) = 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Both of these limits exist. However, they are *not* the same. Consequently, the overall limit at $x=2$ does not exist:

$$

{:db/id 17592186168093 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse hyperbolic functions:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\arsinh}x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\arcosh}x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\artanh}x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\arsinh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\arcosh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\artanh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{5}{2\sqrt{x^2-1}} + 2x \right) \textrm d x
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{5}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}+2x)\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x+\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\text{\arcosh}x+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35388b84-1b96-58fb-b1e8-46477370aa96" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5212 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e1dbdeed-56c4-580b-a139-6581eed4ac8a" :step/math-academy-id 32697 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167590}}] :activity/title "Integration Using Inverse Hyperbolic Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167020} {:db/id 17592186167703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168093 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse hyperbolic functions:

Using Artanh"} :step/id #uuid "a07e3608-4411-5b20-a3f8-e14096686e80" :step/math-academy-id 31172} {:db/id 17592186168093 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse hyperbolic functions:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\arsinh}x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\arcosh}x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\text{\artanh}x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\arsinh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\arcosh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\text{\artanh}x+C, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{5}{2\sqrt{x^2-1}} + 2x \right) \textrm d x
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{5}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}+2x)\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x+\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\text{\arcosh}x+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35388b84-1b96-58fb-b1e8-46477370aa96" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5212 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:course/id #uuid "992cac0c-bf6a-5373-95c9-02edfcfb591e" :course/math-academy-id 105 :db/id 17592186046644} {:db/id 17592186049113 :topic/difficulty 0.6086297348140961 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428510 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & ∗ \\ -3 & ∗\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "From the diagonal matrix $D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ 12 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 12 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$"} {:db/id 17592186125030 :question/id #uuid "6f7410b2-d03a-51b8-bc6b-c6a21e9f2fab" :question/math-academy-id "q-37084"} {:db/id Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

:topic/math-academy-id 1968} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9d/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](images/ca/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](images/3e/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](images/86/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125539 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](images/e1/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fbab2132-0247-5376-a13b-df70908230d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5084 :tutorial/title "Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "620e7d54-99b9-517c-83f8-d408a4768c65" :step/math-academy-id 31837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125540}} {:db/id 17592186125540 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124599 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124411 :question/id #uuid "f7b85641-289b-57b2-9ffc-ff4c5e10025a" :question/math-academy-id "e-8572"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3d7cb0b-7d81-55a5-9781-dda7e9cc9fb9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048775} {:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125086} {:db/id 17592186125088} {:db/id 17592186272005} {:db/id 17592186272006} {:db/id 17592186323864} {:db/id 17592186323876} {:db/id 17592186323926} {:db/id 17592186348381} {:db/id 17592186348382} {:db/id 17592186348383} {:db/id 17592186379810} {:db/id 17592186455441}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable"} :step/id #uuid "62cef711-c61d-5145-9dcc-a1e378b6208e" :step/math-academy-id 31838 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125541}} {:db/id 17592186125541 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125841 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e0a81c7-a393-5e5d-b8c1-16d982404f1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5085 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form"} :step/id #uuid :step/next {:db/id 17592186125539}} {:db/id 17592186125545 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125842 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](images/76/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](images/de/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "eb055132-9c7d-55a5-a2c6-0bcb54877c1c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5086 :tutorial/title "Uniqueness of the Diagonalization"} :step/id #uuid "a11b9aec-3c2f-5a01-8b7c-600351ec33e2" :step/math-academy-id 31854 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125662}} {:db/id 17592186125662 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125896 :tutorial/content "Let ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](images/25/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. ![](images/d8/d8f75220bef8327a8dfc49a6ae22e79c6f1649aefdc8fb43065e0616975a8c5c.svg)
where

- ![](images/1a/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) is an invertible matrix whose columns are eigenvectors ![](images/13/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](images/d0/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) of ![](images/c2/c2c85081d1f89d74b8ebb2761496d211d7052193809b7864e7983437f5d0b80f.svg) and

- ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues ![](images/ff/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and ![](images/4a/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

To understand this better, we need to distinguish between two coordinate systems.

In ![](images/fb/fb3130e489fdca80d1a077702861c20532fe613f9942d48fa1ec24055494a383.svg) the **standard basis** is
![](images/d2/d29d3ee4ae42a8d4ee5304cb0d29c6c811838d7b893a3a831b1b1b8b3af12561.svg)

So, if a vector is written as
![](images/bb/bbbc0379f1691a30dec4c34ec6171db1f116bec12a24891169957af68164f8d3.svg)
then ![](images/12/12adb8ba7ed45d89c9d9a80eb7c06616c41999e9fac57732bc24d2b55e1f8073.svg) The numbers ![](images/34/349015631ec44ef653936c85586d2c5ef56ba64392b3f92b4b92cbef3e731bc5.svg) and ![](images/a7/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) are the *standard coordinates* of ![](images/1f/1f3d1a60926323e963d7563529669e5cf8210771c8cbb0379f7a7d90e7c6aeec.svg)

Now let
![](images/58/58cdfb66e4c93d643fb97273610b3bbf67c8831516d4ccfc5b7790d55a169b28.svg)

![](images/14/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "61524e43-2735-5e5a-904b-2c4973df94a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7958 :tutorial/title "Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "831d0bbd-aa17-5012-9d8b-073e0d2d67a6" :step/math-academy-id 45769}] :activity/title "Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124753} {:db/id 17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9d/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](images/ca/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](images/3e/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](images/86/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](images/e1/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fbab2132-0247-5376-a13b-df70908230d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5084 :tutorial/title "Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "620e7d54-99b9-517c-83f8-d408a4768c65" :step/math-academy-id 31837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125540}} {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e0a81c7-a393-5e5d-b8c1-16d982404f1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5085 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form"} :step/id #uuid "0692f7d4-6f83-540e-bf5f-78b4908292bd" :step/math-academy-id 31841 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125542}} {:db/id 17592186125841 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write
