**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

$P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186404120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404120} :answer-field/id #uuid "5324a7ce-971d-53cb-b107-19a127a08e1f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404115}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f53e1d4c-a53d-5c3e-8ae8-0e080a8e331f" :question/math-academy-id "q-80496" :question/problem "Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}

Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix." :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

$$

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}.
$$

is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0bea5b6f-6c05-5fe2-ad23-ee7c6d0550fe" :step/next {:db/id 17592186499594}} {:db/id 17592186499573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348381 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "188ff12c-cc1a-5287-b72f-b735762cd4d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ is not diagonalizable" :db/id 17592186345568} {:answer/id #uuid "8c4889c1-8a99-5c50-8d21-7e1f3fa8f0f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346569} {:answer/id #uuid "97a5840f-59d5-5c8b-8a78-3953a0ad08a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346680} {:answer/id #uuid "a9bae287-d269-54df-b55a-ae11d68c915d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346833} {:answer/id #uuid "b8d5cbcb-c866-50ca-b5fd-06a7526077af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186346956}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345568} :answer-field/id #uuid "00112189-18a5-5932-8481-85e29798e6dc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347602}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4fad8010-b1d7-51d3-ae7c-0e9c4f636170" :question/math-academy-id "q-80453" :question/problem "Determine if the matrix

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-(-2)I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable."} :step/id #uuid "13e8d76b-e707-545b-91b0-3646c86cd6fd"} {:db/id 17592186499594 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348375 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "218d2232-b6b4-5353-9b44-bc2b615b173f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$a=-5,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-1$" :db/id 17592186345651} {:answer/id #uuid "54242d0d-9f70-50fb-a1c7-1d7500836483" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$a=-1,$ $b=-5,$ and $c=-1$" :db/id 17592186346065} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d2abcd-e82b-5bca-8c24-21c2c07d708d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$a=1,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5$" :db/id 17592186346799} {:answer/id #uuid "a6178168-bb39-5a85-9081-d612835e2505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$a=1,$ $b=-5,$ and $c=-1$" :db/id 17592186346802} {:answer/id #uuid "ff40704f-1d0b-5ea5-8bf6-a3b2c43d0da4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$a=-1,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5$" :db/id 17592186347593}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186345651} :answer-field/id #uuid "e355db22-060d-55f4-890a-5652cc9577f0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348001}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "def1c542-80f5-5b03-88dc-ad7a755f7e8b" :question/math-academy-id "q-80371" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $K$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
K=\begin{bmatrix}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}b & 1 \\ 0 & c\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$

$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}.
$$

is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" :question/math-academy-id "q-138095" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1512bf0f-a0b6-5737-8456-15bf7348d13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414668} {:answer/id #uuid "189d044b-20ef-594f-9050-30d36ea1c805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414669} {:answer/id #uuid "3cba96ef-b9b9-582c-9ce3-fb19b45e7859" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414670} {:answer/id #uuid "b75669b6-5915-5577-8d99-85ede9b169dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414671} {:answer/id #uuid "e53e0f0c-01ad-5114-93c5-0442b0a0663a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186414672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414668} :answer-field/id #uuid "72e392f4-71c8-5797-8085-77f0d25ff7b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414673}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $3.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The  maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}-(-4)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 \\ -5 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186492836 :question/id #uuid "1c7906bc-d806-5034-89ba-962181be4d73" :question/math-academy-id "q-170402" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198443 :knowledge-point/id #uuid 17592186284336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284645 :question/id #uuid "315ff370-acb2-54c0-a94c-7932c53e50d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170525" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58e43fd8-bedb-54d5-9723-4873762018ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186282444} {:answer/id #uuid "6080b967-b1e5-508e-9eb9-b06f08ffc56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186282507} {:answer/id #uuid "b44dda1b-d74d-5302-ac25-2322f81791f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186283250} {:answer/id #uuid "f9c243a3-3d78-5363-a946-67271923a982" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186283874} {:answer/id #uuid "fdac630b-fc7e-5910-8320-fe5c826d997e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186283913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282444} :answer-field/id #uuid "b28de760-832c-5bd3-997a-40bc410c2fcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284244}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284646 :question/id #uuid "40232e39-995b-5a30-a61d-aaa5fd4339dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-170526" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60fcdee7-7ac9-56de-88c2-bc6e649d3116" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186282514} {:answer/id #uuid "8401fb17-15b9-5dc5-a5e7-d89a3bfa1e4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186282829} {:answer/id #uuid "94cc9450-39d8-5e58-92e4-93954393e7bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "54" :db/id 17592186282971} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b2ebcc-3812-51ec-b6fd-80b665e2ed43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186283429} {:answer/id #uuid "f4181463-8020-5bfc-b239-9574c62c514c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186283821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283821} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4313712-6e47-551e-bc79-54931942e74b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284217}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $4{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=16.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -4 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=4$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{4},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -4 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & -8 \\ -16 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}32 & -32 \\ -32 & -16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}32-\lambda  & -32 \\ -32 & -16-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (32-\lambda )(-16-\lambda )-1\,024 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-16\lambda -1\,536 & =0 \\ (\lambda -48)(\lambda +32) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =48,\,-32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186199396}} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/a6/a6165f41eb43e8f6e8fd4399f1c428f73481de9d4b5ec41293f3ec0e4f062fc6.svg)

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/30/30699c4f0abcb099a6f7a76cbd76674757c3f7de313e034d0870d1fce27fdd8c.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](images/ef/ef14ea5facf5010b99721cf915f44162dfa52e089508fb78c2d02d9aad66f1a4.svg)  

Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "08dd4ae6-a6ab-54da-a4ca-840835781b76" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} {:db/id 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "80ab5b9e-fd44-5cd4-b555-7638c14ed974" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410200}} {:db/id 17592186410202 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198560 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5991713d-c756-5033-8e5a-4d4d4ed69367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410175} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd4da5f-a084-569f-9c7d-65ba6f2fa2d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410176} {:answer/id #uuid "7a09264a-e062-5b32-b960-ce1fdd0596f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410180} {:answer/id #uuid "a18e2980-f7b3-5399-bdf5-0e6bab2f2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410183} {:answer/id #uuid "f781d714-082f-5b5c-9033-4f6f86bf4d82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410188}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410176} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a69a67c-d671-56dc-a201-31f05adf2afb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410193}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13f589cb-239b-530f-99ce-e58d907d8d98" :question/math-academy-id "q-136828" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "80ab5b9e-fd44-5cd4-b555-7638c14ed974" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410200}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

"First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

$$

$$

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442118 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2daa7e54-1e63-51fd-a83f-c84ab1ec9d14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442108} {:answer/id #uuid "44864e9b-3b6d-5ead-83f1-bf2b06aa99bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442109} {:answer/id #uuid "47e556d0-ace5-5cd4-bce8-0b8edffbc42a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442110} {:answer/id #uuid "b628a5cd-923e-5683-b6ff-5e0fdf447fc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442111} {:answer/id #uuid "f5d0fa24-c8cf-52e6-90a5-639dbcfbac97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442108} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a8a33df-b62e-5f61-90ea-9cf4c2ac4093" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442113}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "95026062-b044-5134-829b-f9813c55ce41" :question/math-academy-id "q-170503" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-10.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-20)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{bmatrix}+20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}19 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 27\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-20)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442118}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d1abf8ba-5015-5e34-9d28-40c9e16c5051" :answer/type {:db/id $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fea291ee-6497-5ad3-94fc-370909961651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378971} {:answer/id #uuid "d36d82c5-f411-510f-b777-9fca82b43277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378972} {:answer/id #uuid "34611fcc-fc75-5837-8815-4b563c9bc527" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378973} {:answer/id #uuid "a08c13c3-88ad-550d-9cc8-cabd76a06564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378974} {:answer/id #uuid "a6d304bd-fbab-5bd6-8c82-afcb34c6646e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378971} :answer-field/id #uuid "59fbad7d-97f9-581f-9baa-b0e8b8e58fe8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378970}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d3c8fe2-1d6d-57e9-bf5c-5e70cb30abf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-170561" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:
